questions.title: Where exactly does the partition function $Z(x)$ disappear in the DPO derivation?
questions.question_body: I am trying to follow the derivation from Equation 1 (the optimal policy formula) to Equation 4 (the final DPO loss). The paper says 'the partition function cancels' when substituting the reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry model. However, looking at the math, $Z(x)$ appears inside a logarithm in the numerator and denominator separately before becoming a difference. Could someone walk me through the specific algebraic step where $\log Z(x)$ vanishes? I feel like I'm missing a basic property of logarithms or the structure of the preference equation.

questions.title: Why is DPO considered 'stable' if it doesn't use a separate reward model?
questions.question_body: The abstract claims DPO is 'stable' and eliminates the instability of RLHF. Usually, RLHF stability comes from careful tuning of the reward model and PPO clipping. In DPO, we just optimize a single cross-entropy loss directly on the policy. My confusion is: isn't there a risk that without an explicit reward model to regularize things, or without PPO's clipping mechanism, the model could easily collapse to generating only one token? What part of the DPO formulation specifically prevents this mode collapse compared to a naive 'maximize $y_w$ / minimize $y_l$' approach mentioned in the text?

questions.title: Is $\pi_{ref}$ always fixed during training in DPO?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, Algorithm Outline, it mentions initializing $\pi_{ref} = \pi^{SFT}$. Later in Section 4 (Theory), it discusses changing variables. Does $\pi_{ref}$ ever get updated during the gradient descent steps for $\theta$? If I look at Equation 5 ($\mathcal{L}_{DPO}$), it treats $\pi_{ref}$ as a constant denominator. But conceptually, if we are learning a new policy, shouldn't we also be updating what counts as 'reference'? Or is the whole point that keeping it frozen is what makes it equivalent to solving for an optimal policy against a *fixed* KL constraint?

questions.title: How does Theorem 1 guarantee we don't lose expressive power by reparameterizing rewards?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that any reward class consistent with Plackett-Luce can be represented by $r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$. This seems counter-intuitive because usually, reward functions are arbitrary scalars. By forcing them to take this specific log-ratio form relative to $\pi_{ref}$, aren't we implicitly constraining what kind of preferences we can learn? For instance, if the true human preference implies a reward function that grows exponentially with length but not linearly with tokens in a way that fits this ratio... wait, actually, since $\pi(y|x)$ is flexible enough (it's an LM), maybe it covers everything? I just need clarification on why this specific functional form doesn't restrict the set of learnable preference distributions.

questions.title: "Secretly a Reward Model": What is actually being learned here?
questions.question_body: The title says 'Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model'. If I train DPO on my dataset and end up with weights for $\theta$, do these weights encode both the generation strategy AND an implicit reward function simultaneously? If I wanted to extract an explicit reward score for a new sentence later (without generating anything), how would I calculate it using only my trained DPO model and my reference model? Is it just plugging them into that log-ratio formula from Eq 3?
